passage:
A long-standing account of how experiences become enduring memories, known as the standard consolidation model, holds that the hippocampus—a structure buried in the medial temporal lobe—serves as a temporary repository in which a newly formed memory is held while it is gradually transferred to distributed neocortical networks. According to this view, once consolidation is complete, the neocortical trace is self-sufficient, and the hippocampal contribution becomes dispensable. The model is motivated principally by the pattern of retrograde amnesia observed after hippocampal injury: patients typically lose memories formed in the months preceding the injury while retaining memories from years earlier, a temporal gradient that appears to suggest the hippocampus relinquishes its role over time as the neocortical representation matures.

A competing account, the multiple trace theory, accepts that memories come to depend increasingly on the neocortex but denies that the hippocampus is ever wholly bypassed. On this view, each retrieval of an episode reinstates and partially re-encodes the hippocampal trace, so that vivid, context-rich memories continue to recruit the hippocampus even decades after they were formed, with the cumulative number of traces, rather than their individual strength, securing the memory against partial injury. What appears as graded amnesia, proponents argue, is better understood as the loss of the specific, episodic features that depend on hippocampal involvement, while the gist of the same memories—preserved in more distributed neocortical networks—survives.

Evidence from high-resolution neuroimaging has complicated the older picture. Several studies, using activity-pattern analyses rather than simple measures of overall activation, have found that the hippocampus tracks the distinctive details of autobiographical memories regardless of their age, whereas neighboring medial-temporal regions show the temporally graded pattern the standard model predicts. If this distinction is real, then the apparent temporal gradient in lesion data may reflect damage extending beyond the hippocampus proper into these adjacent regions, not the completion of transfer within the hippocampus itself.

Nonetheless, the lesion literature does not fall neatly on either side. Fully developed retrograde gradients have been reported in patients whose damage imaging suggests is largely confined to the hippocampus, and rodent studies using precisely targeted lesions have sometimes reproduced the gradient and sometimes abolished it, depending on how memory is probed. What one concludes about the hippocampus's long-term role turns, accordingly, on whether one regards detail-rich recollection and schematic recall as expressions of the same underlying memory or of distinct representations supported by different substrates. The evidence at present is more consistent with the latter possibility than with the former, though a single experiment decisive between the two, one that could dissociate these two features under a hippocampus-only lesion, has not yet been reported.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that the hippocampus, contrary to earlier assumptions, plays no specialized role in the retention of autobiographical memories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because retrograde amnesia after hippocampal injury follows a temporal gradient, the standard consolidation model is more consistent with clinical data than its rivals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the hippocampus remains necessary for remote memory depends on whether detail-rich recollection and schematic recall are treated as a single process, and the current evidence favors treating them as distinct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activity-pattern analyses of neuroimaging data should replace lesion studies as the primary basis for theories of memory consolidation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rodent studies using targeted hippocampal lesions have settled the debate over whether remote memories remain hippocampus-dependent.

explanations.correct: The passage contrasts two models, presents neuroimaging and lesion evidence that pulls in different directions, and closes by framing the choice between them as turning on whether detailed and schematic recall are one representation or two—noting that current evidence is 'more consistent with the latter possibility.' C captures both strands.
explanations.A: Overreach. The passage treats the hippocampus as plausibly retaining a role for detailed recollection; it does not deny a specialized role.
explanations.B: Reverses the author's final assessment. The author says current evidence is more consistent with multiple trace theory than with the standard model.
explanations.D: Methodological reform of this kind is not the passage's thesis; imaging is described as complicating the picture, not as replacing other methods.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly states rodent results cut both ways depending on how memory is probed, and that a decisive experiment 'has not yet been reported.'

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prevailing model is described together with its motivating evidence; a competing model is introduced; a body of newer evidence is shown to complicate the prevailing model; ambiguities in the older evidence are acknowledged; the author states which position the present evidence better supports.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A long-standing model is described; newer evidence is shown to refute it decisively; a replacement model is endorsed without reservation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing models are introduced; each is shown to be inadequate in light of a third alternative, which the author defends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A methodological problem in memory research is posed; competing remedies are surveyed; the author recommends adopting high-resolution neuroimaging as the solution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An experimental finding is reported; two interpretations of it are developed in parallel; the author concludes that the finding cannot be interpreted without further data.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1: standard model + its motivating lesion evidence. Paragraph 2: competing multiple trace theory. Paragraph 3: newer neuroimaging evidence complicating the standard model. Paragraph 4: acknowledgment that lesion data does not cleanly favor either side, followed by the author's qualified assessment.
explanations.B: Misstates the conclusion: the author says current evidence is 'more consistent' with the alternative, not that the standard model is decisively refuted.
explanations.C: There is no third alternative in the passage; the author's closing assessment favors one of the two introduced models.
explanations.D: Methodology is not the organizing concern; neuroimaging is one line of evidence among several.
explanations.E: The passage does not decline to interpret the evidence; it reaches a qualified conclusion.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The temporal gradient observed in retrograde amnesia may reflect injury to regions adjacent to the hippocampus rather than a completed transfer of memories out of the hippocampus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Once a memory has been consolidated in the neocortex, it cannot be further modified by subsequent retrievals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autobiographical memories lose their detailed features as soon as they are no longer dependent on hippocampal activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard consolidation model's prediction about the hippocampus is better supported by rodent data than by human data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring medial-temporal regions contribute nothing distinctive to the retention of autobiographical memories.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that if activity-pattern analyses are right that the hippocampus tracks detail regardless of age, then 'the apparent temporal gradient in lesion data may reflect damage extending beyond the hippocampus proper, not the completion of transfer within it.' A is a near paraphrase.
explanations.B: The multiple trace theory's re-encoding claim, which the author treats sympathetically, is inconsistent with this.
explanations.C: The passage treats loss of detail as an alternative interpretation of graded amnesia, not as a general fact about autobiographical memories.
explanations.D: Rodent studies are described as cutting both ways; the author does not say rodent data favor the standard model more strongly.
explanations.E: The passage notes that neighboring regions 'show the temporally graded pattern the standard model predicts,' which implies they do contribute distinctively.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion, in the third paragraph, of activity-pattern analyses functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a methodological advance whose results call into question an inference drawn from the older lesion evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede a limitation of the multiple trace theory that its proponents have not adequately addressed

choices.label: C
choices.text: summarize a finding that both competing models have already incorporated

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a third hypothesis that the author will ultimately defend

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why overall measures of brain activation have historically been preferred to activity-pattern analyses

explanations.correct: The paragraph presents activity-pattern analyses as a newer method (a methodological advance) whose results—hippocampus tracking detail regardless of age—call into question the inference, drawn from the lesion gradient, that the hippocampus relinquishes its role.
explanations.B: Activity-pattern results are introduced on the side of the multiple trace theory, not as a concession against it.
explanations.C: The passage presents the finding as complicating the 'older picture'; it has not been absorbed by both models.
explanations.E: The passage implies the opposite—activity-pattern analyses have revealed something overall activation did not—without asserting which was historically preferred.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that a proponent of the multiple trace theory would most likely regard a patient who retains the gist of events from a decade earlier but cannot recall their specific details as

choices.label: A
choices.text: evidence that the hippocampus transfers memories completely to the neocortex once consolidation is finished

choices.label: B
choices.text: evidence that detail-rich and schematic features of a memory depend on different substrates, only one of which has been disrupted

choices.label: C
choices.text: evidence that activity-pattern analyses overstate the hippocampus's role in remote memory

choices.label: D
choices.text: evidence that retrograde amnesia gradients are methodological artifacts of how memory is probed in rodents

choices.label: E
choices.text: evidence that neocortical networks are not themselves involved in the retention of autobiographical memories

explanations.correct: Multiple trace theory holds that detailed, context-rich recall recruits the hippocampus while gist survives in distributed neocortical networks. A patient with preserved gist but lost detail is, on that view, evidence that the two features are supported by different substrates, one of which has been disrupted.
explanations.A: That is the standard consolidation model's reading, which multiple trace theory rejects.
explanations.C: Activity-pattern analyses are cited in support of multiple trace theory; proponents would not use the pattern against that evidence.
explanations.D: Rodent methodology is not the multiple trace theorist's explanation of the human pattern described.
explanations.E: Both models hold that neocortex is involved; the theorist would not dispute that.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's qualified assessment in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new technique demonstrates that, in patients with damage confined to the hippocampus alone, both the detail-rich and the schematic features of remote autobiographical memories are lost together in the same graded pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rodent studies using targeted hippocampal lesions show that animals can still learn new spatial tasks after the lesion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A case study reports a patient whose hippocampal damage is accompanied by marked impairment in forming new memories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activity-pattern analyses reveal that regions outside the medial temporal lobe also track the distinctive details of autobiographical memories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A proponent of the standard consolidation model concedes that retrieval partially reinstates the hippocampal trace.

explanations.correct: The author's assessment depends on treating detail-rich recollection and schematic recall as distinct representations supported by different substrates; a hippocampus-only lesion that abolishes both together in the same graded pattern would undercut that distinction and thus weaken the author's case for multiple trace theory.
explanations.B: Anterograde task learning is a different question from retrograde retention; the author's claim is about remote autobiographical memory, not new learning.
explanations.C: Impaired encoding after hippocampal damage is consistent with both models and does not bear on the author's remote-memory claim.
explanations.D: Additional regions tracking detail would not undercut the author's claim that the hippocampus also does so; it would just broaden the distributed trace.
explanations.E: A partial concession by the standard model's defenders moves in the author's direction, not against it.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following research scenarios most closely conforms to the reasoning the author employs in evaluating the two models of memory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An ecologist observes that a predator population declines after a habitat change, concludes the change is responsible, and dismisses alternative explanations without testing them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A geneticist, confronted with two hypotheses about a trait's inheritance, notes that a pattern in pedigree data is consistent with both and proposes a cellular-level mechanism that would distinguish the two, provisionally favoring the hypothesis more compatible with recent mechanistic findings while acknowledging that a decisive test has not been run.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chemist selects between two reaction mechanisms on the basis of computational modeling alone, ignoring the experimental yields reported in earlier studies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physicist reports an anomaly and defers any interpretation of it until a theoretical framework addressing it has been worked out.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A clinician, finding that two treatments produce similar outcomes in a small trial, recommends whichever is less expensive and abandons further investigation of their mechanisms.

explanations.correct: The author weighs lesion data consistent with both models, introduces a newer mechanistic line of evidence (activity-pattern analyses) that distinguishes them, and provisionally favors the hypothesis better supported by that evidence while noting that no decisive experiment has been run. B mirrors each of these moves.
explanations.A: The author does not dismiss alternatives; both models are engaged with throughout.
explanations.C: The author explicitly relies on empirical studies, not modeling alone.
explanations.D: The author reaches a qualified conclusion rather than deferring interpretation.
explanations.E: The author does not choose on extra-evidential grounds like cost, and does investigate underlying mechanisms.

passage:
Hot Jupiters—gas giants orbiting their host stars at distances a small fraction of the Earth-Sun separation—are, on any reasonable accounting, losing atmosphere to space. What has remained contested is the dominant mechanism driving that loss, and the dispute bears directly on whether the planets observed today began as still larger bodies or have roughly retained their original mass.

One account, energy-limited escape, treats the process as a balance sheet: extreme ultraviolet radiation from the star deposits energy in the upper atmosphere, and some fraction of that energy is converted into the work required to lift gas out of the planet's gravitational well. Because the stellar ultraviolet flux scales with proximity and is known to decline by roughly an order of magnitude over the first billion years of a Sun-like star's life, an energy-limited calculation predicts that a hot Jupiter formed near its present orbit would have shed, at most, a few percent of its initial mass. On this view, today's population of hot Jupiters looks approximately as it has always looked.

A second account, hydrodynamic outflow driven by Roche-lobe overflow, is less forgiving. When a planet's upper atmosphere is heated enough to expand beyond the surface at which the star's gravity becomes the stronger pull (the Roche limit), gas ceases to be retained and streams away in a hydrodynamic wind whose rate is set not by radiative energy alone but by the planet's thermal structure and surface gravity. Simulations of this regime suggest that an inflated young hot Jupiter—larger and lower-density at formation than after cooling—could have lost a substantial fraction of its envelope before contracting to its present radius. If so, a meaningful share of the currently observed hot Jupiters were originally more massive objects.

The discriminating evidence ought to be a population statistic: if envelope-stripping is important, there should be a measurable deficit of hot Jupiters at the masses most vulnerable to it, a 'desert' in the mass-orbit plane around stars old enough for the process to have run to completion. Such a deficit has been reported in several surveys, though its boundaries are not sharp, and critics note that the same region is populated sparsely for reasons independent of escape, since planets of those masses are harder to detect at short periods around certain spectral types.

What can be said with some confidence is that neither mechanism alone captures the range of outcomes observed: energy-limited escape is adequate for many middle-aged systems but understates losses during the first few hundred million years, while hydrodynamic outflow is appropriate for inflated young planets but overpredicts losses once cooling and contraction have set in. A synthesis in which the dominant channel shifts with age would accommodate both the observed mass distribution and the fact that measured present-day escape rates are, in most cases, modest. Whether that synthesis will survive further data is another matter.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent surveys have established that most observed hot Jupiters began as substantially more massive planets that have since lost large fractions of their envelopes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the extreme ultraviolet flux of Sun-like stars declines sharply over their first billion years, hot Jupiters orbiting older stars are losing negligible amounts of mass today.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two mechanisms of atmospheric escape from hot Jupiters make sharply different predictions about their original masses, and the available evidence favors a synthesis in which the dominant mechanism depends on the planet's age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The apparent deficit of hot Jupiters at certain masses is more plausibly explained by detection biases than by any escape mechanism.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrodynamic outflow models should be abandoned because they overpredict mass loss in cooled and contracted hot Jupiters.

explanations.correct: The passage presents two mechanisms with opposing implications for original mass, reviews evidence that cuts both ways, and concludes that a synthesis in which the dominant channel shifts with age fits the data best. C captures each element.
explanations.A: Overstates the survey results; the passage calls the deficit's boundaries 'not sharp' and notes alternative explanations.
explanations.B: A subsidiary claim of only one of the two models, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.D: The passage treats detection biases as one consideration among several, not as the preferred explanation.
explanations.E: The author does not reject hydrodynamic outflow; the synthesis incorporates it for young, inflated planets.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a prediction of the energy-limited escape account?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inflated young hot Jupiter will lose gas at a rate set primarily by its thermal structure rather than by radiative input.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dominant channel of mass loss in hot Jupiters shifts with the planet's age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hot Jupiter that formed near its present orbit would have lost only a small fraction of its initial mass over the first billion years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A deficit of hot Jupiters at certain masses will be observed around stars old enough for escape processes to have run to completion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hot Jupiters initially retain their mass despite exposure to extreme ultraviolet radiation, because that radiation does no work against their gravity.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2: energy-limited calculations, given the roughly order-of-magnitude decline in stellar ultraviolet flux, predict that 'a hot Jupiter formed near its present orbit would have shed, at most, a few percent of its initial mass.' C paraphrases that prediction.
explanations.A: That is hydrodynamic outflow's account, not energy-limited escape's.
explanations.B: The age-dependent shift is the author's proposed synthesis, not a prediction of the energy-limited model alone.
explanations.D: The mass-deficit prediction belongs to the envelope-stripping account; energy-limited escape predicts small losses and thus no substantial deficit.
explanations.E: Reverses the model's logic: in energy-limited escape, some fraction of the ultraviolet energy is converted into the work of lifting gas out; losses are small but not zero.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to detection difficulties in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede a consideration that weakens the inference from the observed mass deficit to the importance of envelope-stripping escape

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that the reported mass deficit is entirely an artifact of the methods used to discover short-period planets

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a third mechanism of atmospheric escape that neither of the previous accounts has addressed

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate how the stellar ultraviolet flux varies with spectral type

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why hot Jupiters are more common around older stars than around younger ones

explanations.correct: Having introduced the mass deficit as potentially discriminating evidence for envelope-stripping, the author concedes that the same region is populated sparsely for reasons independent of escape, thereby weakening the inference from the deficit to envelope-stripping's importance.
explanations.B: The concession is qualified (the boundaries are 'not sharp,' critics 'note' an alternative); the passage does not assert the deficit is 'entirely an artifact.'
explanations.C: No third mechanism is introduced here.
explanations.D: Spectral-type variation in ultraviolet flux is not the paragraph's topic.
explanations.E: The passage does not make claims about the relative commonness of hot Jupiters by stellar age.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following inferences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Energy-limited escape predicts greater cumulative mass loss than hydrodynamic outflow does over a planet's first few hundred million years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The present-day radius of a hot Jupiter is independent of the mechanism by which it has lost mass in the past.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hot Jupiter's susceptibility to Roche-lobe overflow is greater before it has cooled and contracted than after.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extreme ultraviolet flux received by a planet in a fixed orbit remains approximately constant over the host star's main-sequence lifetime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Present-day escape rates measured for hot Jupiters are generally large enough, if sustained, to remove most of a planet's envelope over a billion years.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says hydrodynamic outflow operates when the atmosphere expands beyond the Roche limit and that an 'inflated young hot Jupiter—larger and lower-density at formation than after cooling' could lose a substantial envelope; paragraph 5 says hydrodynamic outflow 'overpredicts losses once cooling and contraction have set in.' Together, these support C.
explanations.A: Reverses the relationship; the author says energy-limited escape 'understates losses' in the first few hundred million years.
explanations.B: The passage treats radius and mass-loss history as linked: inflation during early losses is precisely what drives hydrodynamic outflow.
explanations.D: The passage says ultraviolet flux declines by roughly an order of magnitude over the first billion years, contradicting constancy.
explanations.E: The final paragraph says present-day escape rates are 'in most cases, modest,' the opposite of large enough to remove most of an envelope if sustained.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the proposed synthesis described in the final paragraph is most accurately characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement without reservation

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified endorsement, with an acknowledgment that further evidence could displace it

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissive skepticism grounded in detection biases

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral reportage without any evaluative stance

choices.label: E
choices.text: approval of the synthesis's underlying methodology combined with rejection of its specific predictions

explanations.correct: The author presents the synthesis as accommodating the data better than either mechanism alone ('would accommodate both... measured present-day escape rates are, in most cases, modest'), but closes with 'Whether that synthesis will survive further data is another matter,' a characteristic LSAT hedge.
explanations.A: The closing sentence is explicitly a reservation.
explanations.C: The synthesis is endorsed provisionally, not dismissed.
explanations.D: The author evaluates both mechanisms and favors the synthesis; this is not neutral reportage.
explanations.E: The author approves of the synthesis's predictions for current data; nothing in the passage rejects specific predictions while approving methodology.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's claim that a synthesis in which the dominant escape channel shifts with age is preferable to either mechanism alone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of young, inflated hot Jupiters finds measured escape rates substantially higher than energy-limited models predict, while a survey of older, contracted hot Jupiters finds rates close to those same models' predictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simulations show that hydrodynamic outflow can be driven by stellar winds rather than by radiative heating alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The extreme ultraviolet flux from Sun-like stars declines more slowly than previously estimated over their first billion years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detection techniques for short-period planets around certain spectral types have improved enough to remove the apparent mass deficit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A newly discovered hot Jupiter has no detectable atmospheric escape despite orbiting a young star.

explanations.correct: The author's synthesis claims hydrodynamic outflow dominates for inflated young planets and energy-limited escape for older ones. A finding that young inflated planets show losses exceeding energy-limited predictions, while older contracted planets match those predictions, directly instantiates this age-dependent shift.
explanations.B: A wind-driven variant of hydrodynamic outflow does not bear on the claim that the dominant channel shifts with age.
explanations.C: A slower UV decline affects the inputs to energy-limited escape but does not support the age-dependent shift.
explanations.D: Removing the mass deficit would undermine a separate strand of evidence for envelope-stripping, not support the synthesis.
explanations.E: A single counterexample to young-planet escape would complicate, not support, the synthesis's claim that hydrodynamic outflow dominates for inflated young planets.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the kind of reasoning by which the author evaluates the reported mass deficit as evidence for envelope-stripping?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A seismologist concludes that the scarcity of large earthquakes along a fault segment is due to the segment's low slip rate, but an interlocutor notes that few large earthquakes would be expected there anyway given the fault's short recorded history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A botanist claims that a rare plant's distribution is explained by soil chemistry and rejects any role for climatic variables.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An economist predicts that a tax change will raise revenue and defends the prediction by citing unrelated historical cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An astronomer reports a new exoplanet and argues that its mere existence confirms the theory that predicted it, without considering alternative theories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A chemist measures reaction rates under controlled conditions and concludes that the measured values apply to industrial-scale reactions.

explanations.correct: The author entertains the mass deficit as evidence for envelope-stripping but concedes that the same region is populated sparsely for independent reasons (detection difficulty), weakening the inference from the deficit to its purported cause. A mirrors this: a pattern is proposed as evidence for a mechanism, but a rival explanation (short recorded history) predicts the pattern independently.
explanations.B: The botanist dismisses an alternative rather than weighing it as the author does.
explanations.C: Citation of unrelated cases is not parallel to entertaining an independent explanation of the same pattern.
explanations.D: The astronomer ignores alternatives; the author explicitly raises one.
explanations.E: Extrapolation from laboratory to industrial scale does not mirror the structure of entertaining a competing explanation for the same observation.
